newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian airlines lost $220 million in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Russian airlines lost $220 million in 1996.

text.p: Russian airlines lost more than $200 million last year and 118 carriers went out of business because fewer passengers could afford to fly than in 1995, statistics released Thursday showed.
The poor results, which followed a profitable 1995, coincided with a 15 percent fall in passengers numbers, the Federal Aviation Service said in a report.
"It was a very difficult year for Russian civil aviation," Gennady Zaitsev, the service's director told his agency's annual board meeting. "We hoped that 1996 results would be better."
He said 118 Russian airlines lost permission to operate in 1996 and another 58 carriers may soon be join the list.
Nearly 200 Russian airlines, most created out of the domestic routes of the old Aeroflot aviation monopoly following the fall of communism, have gone out of business in the last three years, he said.
Zaitsev said 328 airlines had the right to operate regular and charter flights in Russia, compared with 520 carriers three years ago.
Experts blame the industry's woes on Russia's economic problems and Zaitsev said airlines remained in deep crisis.
Officials from several carriers also said that high fuel and landing fees hurt them in 1996.
"In 1996 there were very high fuel and airport charges practically everywhere in Russia," said Oleg Solovyov, flight director of Vnukovo Airlines, one of the largest domestic carriers.
He said his airline suffered from non-payment from tour operators who leased their jets for charter flights.
The report showed that Russian airlines lost a total of $213 million in 1996, compared with a profit of about $76 million in 1995.
Zaitsev said passenger traffic dropped 13 percent to 26.9 million passengers last year from 31 million in 1995, partly because of higher ticket costs.
